prompt: The client asks: "Should we offer a 20% discount for paying a year up front?" Fact sheet: the monthly plan is $50; the average monthly customer stays 9 months; the annual plan at 20% off would be $480; 40% of surveyed customers would choose the annual plan; in a past test, customers who chose an annual plan had stayed about as long as average; the company is opening an office in Austin. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Don't offer it. Customers who'd pay $600 a year monthly would pay only $480, a 20% loss.
options.feedback: It ignores that the average monthly customer stays 9 months and pays $450, less than $480.

options.text: Offer the annual plan. With a new office opening in Austin, cash up front will help fund it.
options.feedback: The Austin office doesn't decide this. The $480 against $450 comparison does.

options.text: The annual plan raises cash up front but may cut revenue from loyal customers. The call is a balanced one.
options.feedback: This never commits, even though the average customer pays less than $480.

options.text: Offer the annual plan. $480 up front beats the $450 the average monthly customer pays over 9 months.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and compares revenue per customer.

explanation: Full answer: Offer the annual plan at 20% off. An annual customer pays $480 up front, more than the $450 the average monthly customer pays over 9 months, and in a past test annual buyers had stayed about as long as average. The main risk is that some loyal customers who would pay $600 a year switch to $480, so the next step is to offer it to new customers first and compare lifetime revenue. What would change the answer: annual buyers turning out to be mostly customers who would have stayed a year anyway.

irrelevant_facts: The company is opening an office in Austin.
